    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ovariancancer.html">
      <content name="title">Ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Fallopian Tube <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Primary <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Peritoneal</span></span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> is a disease in which abnormal cells in the body grow out of control and form a <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">tumor</span></span>. Ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is a cancerous <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">tumor</span></span> that forms in the tissues of an ovary. The ovaries are a pair of female reproductive glands that make eggs and female hormones.</p>What are the types of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>There are a few different types of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. The most common type is epithelial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. It begins in the cells that cover the ovary.</p><p>There are also two related types of epithelial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> that can spread to the ovaries:</p><ul><li>Fallopian tube <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> forms in the tissue lining a fallopian tube. The fallopian tubes are a pair of long, slender tubes on each side of the uterus. The uterus is the female reproductive organ where a fetus grows during pregnancy.</li><li>Primary <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneal</span></span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> forms in the tissue lining the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneum</span></span>. Your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneum</span></span> is a tissue lining that covers the organs in the abdomen (belly).</li></ul><p>These two <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> are like ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, and they have the same treatments. So some medical experts also consider those two types as ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Some other rarer types of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> are malignant germ cell <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">tumors</span></span> and stromal <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">tumors</span></span>.</p>What causes ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>Ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes (mutations) in the genetic material  (DNA). Often, the exact cause of these genetic changes is unknown.</p><p>Most ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span> are caused by genetic changes that happen during your lifetime. But sometimes these genetic changes are inherited, meaning that you are born with them. Ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> that is caused by inherited genetic changes is called hereditary ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>There are also certain genetic changes that can raise your risk of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, including changes called BRCA1 and BRCA2. These two changes also raise your risk of breast and other <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancers</span></span>.</p><p>Besides genetics, your lifestyle and the environment can affect your risk of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>Certain people are more likely to develop ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. They include those who:</p><ul><li>Have a family history of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> in a mother, aunt, grandmother, or sister</li><li>Have inherited changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes</li><li>Have certain other genetic conditions, such as Lynch syndrome</li><li>Have endometriosis</li><li>Took hormone therapy for menopause</li><li>Are overweight or have obesity</li><li>Are tall</li><li>Are older, especially those who have gone through menopause</li><li>Have never been pregnant</li></ul>What are the symptoms of ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>Ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> may not cause early signs or symptoms. By the time you do have signs or symptoms, the <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is often advanced.</p><p>The signs and symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Pain, swelling, or a feeling of pressure in the abdomen (belly) or pelvis</li><li>Sudden or frequent urge to urinate (pee)</li><li>Trouble eating or feeling full</li><li>A lump in the pelvic area</li><li>Gastrointestinal problems, such as gas, bloating, or constipation</li></ul>How is ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your medical history, including your symptoms</li><li>Will ask about your family health history, including relatives who have had ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span></li><li>Will do a physical exam, including a pelvic exam</li><li>Will likely do imaging tests</li><li>May do blood tests such as a CA-125 blood test</li></ul><p>Often the only way to know for sure that you have ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> is by having a biopsy of the tissue. A biopsy is done during surgery to remove the <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">tumor</span></span>.</p>What are the treatments for ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatments for ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> may include:</p><ul><li>Surgery to remove as much of the <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> as possible</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>Your provider may suggest that you have genetic testing to look for the gene changes that raise the risk for ovarian <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">cancer</span></span>. Knowing whether you have the gene change may help your provider decide on your treatment plan.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="altTitle">Peritonitis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneum</span></span> is the tissue that lines your abdominal wall and covers most of the organs in your abdomen. A liquid, <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneal</span></span> fluid, lubricates the surface of this tissue.</p><p>Disorders of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneum</span></span> are not common. They include:</p><ul><li>Peritonitis - an inflammation of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneum</span></span></li><li><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Cancer</span></span></li><li>Complications from <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneal</span></span> dialysis</li></ul><p>Your doctor may use imaging tests or lab tests to analyze the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneal</span></span> fluid to diagnose the problem. Treatment of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">peritoneal</span></span> disorders depends on the cause.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/kidneyfailure.html">
      <content name="title">Kidney Failure</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ESRD</content>
      <content name="altTitle">End-Stage Renal Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Renal Failure</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Healthy kidneys clean your blood by removing excess fluid, minerals, and wastes. They also make hormones that keep your bones strong and your blood healthy. But if the kidneys are damaged, they don't work properly. Harmful wastes can build up in your body. Your blood pressure may rise. Your body may retain excess fluid and not make enough red blood cells. This is called kidney failure.</p><p>If your kidneys fail, you need treatment to replace the work they normally do. The treatment options are dialysis or a kidney transplant. Each treatment has benefits and drawbacks. No matter which treatment you choose, you'll need to make some changes in your life, including how you eat and plan your activities. But with the help of health care providers, family, and friends, most people with kidney failure can lead full and active lives.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Wounds and Injuries</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Accidents</content>

      <content name="altTitle">Lacerations</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Traumatic injuries</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>An injury is damage to your body. It is a general term that refers to harm caused by accidents, falls, hits, weapons, and more. In the U.S., millions of people injure themselves every year. These injuries range from minor to life-threatening. Injuries can happen at work or play, indoors or outdoors, driving a car, or walking across the street.</p><p>Wounds are injuries that break the skin or other body tissues.   They include cuts, scrapes, scratches, and punctured skin. They often happen because of an accident, but surgery, sutures, and stitches also cause wounds. Minor wounds usually aren't serious, but it is important to clean them. Serious and infected wounds may require first aid followed by a visit to your doctor. You should also seek attention if the wound is deep, you cannot close it yourself, you cannot stop the bleeding or get the dirt out, or it does not heal.</p><p>Other common types of injuries include:</p><ul><li>Animal bites</li><li>Bruises</li><li>Burns</li><li>Dislocations</li><li>Electrical injuries</li><li>Fractures (broken bones)</li><li>Sprains and strains</li></ul></content>
